initial_requirements: Web-archiving institutions need an expanded WARC Tools suite for managing large collections of archived web content. Archivists and engineers should be able to configure and run migrations from ARC to WARC, repackage collections, inspect and browse records, produce reports, detect duplicates, and verify content and metadata after conversion. The tools should support collaborative deployment and testing across institutions and scale to large collection batches.

slots.key: Definition of successful conversion and validation
slots.value: Content and metadata are verified after conversion, with checks on what changed after conversion; archivists also need to be able to inspect and browse records when something looks odd. A successful transition also means staff can keep doing the same core jobs without jumping between ad hoc scripts and manual checks, and the results are trustworthy enough to use in production workflows. Results that are close enough to look valid but not trustworthy enough for production use should be clearly flagged; hard validation failures should block downstream use until someone reviews them; borderline results or those with warnings should be routed to manual review so staff can decide whether they are acceptable. Automatic fix-up should be limited to small, well-understood issues like minor formatting irregularities that don’t change the meaning of the record, or missing bits that can be safely normalized. Corruption, truncated content, broken headers, or ambiguous metadata should go to staff triage. Conversion can proceed with non-fatal, clearly documented validation errors only when the tool can preserve enough context for later review; if output may be misleading or not trustworthy, the process should stop or require explicit confirmation before continuing. Staff use WARC and ARC record data for quality control and preservation checking to confirm the archive is complete, readable, and suitable for long-term access or migration, and also to diagnose problems, explain anomalies in reports, and verify that conversion didn’t change anything unexpectedly. Records should be complete and internally consistent, with headers, payload, and metadata agreeing; redirects, embedded resources, duplicate captures, and slightly unusual formatting can often be handled automatically, but truncated, corrupt, or contradictory records that affect trust should trigger human review. For reporting and verification, tools should capture and display record identifier, capture date and time, source file or batch, record type, target URI or URL, basic size or checksum information if available, conversion status, warnings, and the relationship between source record and output record so staff can trace lineage. For special cases, redirect location, duplicate match information, and an incomplete-record flag should be visible when relevant, especially for incomplete or duplicated records, though there is not yet a hard rule that any one of those fields is universally mandatory in every case. When output falls short, the batch should be marked as partially successful or failed depending on the size of the gap, and detailed error information should remain attached; it should not be promoted to a clean success unless the missing pieces are clearly accounted for and consciously accepted. It should recognize at least the WARC version, any declared profile, and the record structure differences that affect headers, payload handling, and metadata fields. The key requirement is to preserve whatever variant information is already present so we don’t silently normalize away details that matter for downstream use or comparison. Common, supported variants should be accepted with normal processing, unusual or only partially supported variants should generate warnings, and variants that would change the meaning of the records or prevent reliable validation and browsing should be rejected as incompatible. The tool should be explicit about what it could convert, what it had to skip, and what it repaired or normalized, so archivists can tell when output is faithful versus compromised and decide whether manual review is needed.

slots.key: Conversion error handling and restart behavior
slots.value: Needs tools that can repack, inspect, deduplicate, verify content, validate converted files, and run jobs reliably so staff can configure a job, run the migration or repackaging, verify the output, generate useful reports, and check what changed after conversion without troubleshooting every batch by hand; current practice includes inspecting output, comparing counts or metadata, and sometimes rerunning pieces if something looks off. For anything that fails the core validation checks, the tool should block downstream use until someone reviews it. Borderline results or results with warnings rather than hard failures should be routed to manual review so staff can decide whether they are acceptable for that collection. Conversion can proceed with some validation errors if they’re non-fatal and clearly documented, but only when the tool can preserve enough context for later review; if there’s any risk that the output would be misleading or not trustworthy, the process should stop or require explicit confirmation before continuing. A batch should only count as successful if the required conversion and verification steps are complete for everything that was in scope, not just most of it. If there are exceptions, they need to be small, understood, and explicitly accepted by the workflow rather than quietly ignored. When the output falls short, the tool should mark the batch as partially successful or failed, depending on how serious the gap is, and keep the detailed error information attached. It should not promote the batch to a clean success state unless the missing pieces are clearly accounted for and someone has made a conscious decision to accept them. The tool should be restartable from the last completed point after an interruption rather than starting over. A safe-resume warning or block should trigger if the tool can’t reliably confirm that the last checkpoint is still valid, if the output directory already contains records matching the same source items without a clear completion marker, or if the configuration, tool version, or source set has changed since the earlier run. If there is any sign of duplicate output, truncated files, or mixed results from different settings, it should not resume automatically and must force human review before cleanup or explicit restart approval. If a batch fails partway through, retry only the failed portion when the tool can prove the completed items are intact and won’t be duplicated; otherwise stop and require a manual decision rather than risking inconsistent output. When access or connection is interrupted during a transfer or write, the tool must record exactly what was completed, what was left incomplete, and the point where the failure happened, and write a recovery status that is easy to read in logs and reports, including any rerun steps or cleanup needed before retrying.

slots.value: The receiving team should be able to see exactly what was done, what remains unprocessed, and what assumptions were applied; local overrides must be explicit and not hidden. For a normal completed run, they probably only need a concise summary, but for partial runs, reruns, or mixed-source jobs they need much more detail about what was processed, what was skipped, any overrides or local assumptions that affected the result, the exact job state, the boundaries of each processed segment, and any warnings about data that may not compare cleanly across sources. The goal is that the receiving team can take over without having to reconstruct the workflow from logs. Archivists need to know when the output is faithful and when there was a compromise so they can decide whether a collection needs manual review.

slots.key: Tolerance for interrupted jobs and recovery expectations
slots.value: Jobs should be batch-aligned to source collection boundaries whenever possible for clearer tracking and reporting. When collections are too large, subdivision by file count or size limit is allowed, but batch layout should be deterministic so the same inputs produce the same results. If a batch fails partway through, the tool should retry only the failed portion if it can prove completed items are intact and won’t be duplicated. If it cannot prove that, it should stop and require a manual decision rather than risking inconsistent output. If access or connection is interrupted, it should pause or stop in a way that lets staff recover without guessing what was already committed and what still needs to be rerun. It should also record exactly what was completed, what was left incomplete, and the point where the failure happened, so staff can tell whether they need to rerun the whole job or just the failed part. For collaborative handoff during ARC to WARC conversion, the receiving team should see a concise summary for a normal completed run, but much more detail for partial runs, reruns, or mixed-source jobs, including the exact job state, boundaries of each processed segment, what was processed or skipped, any local assumptions or overrides, and warnings about data that may not compare cleanly across sources so they can take over without reconstructing the workflow from logs. The split should be reproducible from the original batch definition, and the tool should record exactly how the cut was made, including the file count or size threshold and the ordering rule used, so a later retry doesn’t reshuffle things. For a partial retry, there should be proof that the failed segment is isolated and that the successful pieces are already verified and immutable; if there is any ambiguity about whether the split changed the package content or the failure might have affected upstream records, the job should go to manual review instead of retrying automatically.

slots.value: Staff need understandable messages, examples of common fixes, and enough context in reports to explain results to colleagues without specialized expertise. Reports should be readable and use consistent terminology so teams can tell what happened, why a job failed or produced a warning, and support day-to-day troubleshooting. They should include plain-language summaries alongside technical details, plus record counts, duplicate findings, validation results, and short explanations of errors or warnings in archivist-friendly terms. Reports should also clearly show the source collection, the run configuration, and the reason for any skipped or failed items so a colleague can understand the outcome without digging through logs or internal processing steps. On failure, the tool should log the reason in plain terms and not leave half-written outputs looking complete. It should also write a recovery status that is easy to read in logs and reports, including any rerun steps or cleanup needed before retrying. slots.key: Acceptance criteria for migration and verification
slots.value: Content and metadata are verified after conversion; staff can run migration jobs reliably, check what changed after conversion, browse records when something looks odd, and produce shareable reports. Shared terminology for success criteria is needed, including what counts as a successful migration, a valid record, or a reportable error, and tools should present consistent terminology. The tool should support shared presets or profiles for the core conversion and verification rules so each institution can run the same logic even if its local workflow differs. It should preserve the full job history, tool version, and configuration used so another team can reproduce or compare results later. On handoff, the receiving team must be able to see exactly what was done, what remains unprocessed, and what assumptions were applied, and any local overrides must be explicit and not hidden. The tools should give plain-language summaries alongside the technical details, so someone can quickly see what was processed, what changed, and whether anything needs attention, including record counts, duplicate findings, validation results, and short explanations of errors or warnings in archivist-friendly language. Reports should clearly show the source collection, the run configuration, and the reason for any skipped or failed items so a colleague can understand the outcome without digging through logs or knowing the internal processing steps. Institution-specific packaging rules should be configurable rather than hardcoded, and acceptable packages should follow required output profiles, naming and directory conventions, carry forward source identifiers, collection identifiers, and required metadata, and pass the institution’s validation steps such as completeness checks, metadata checks, fixity checks, and duplicate checks. Any local rule that conflicts with the shared conversion or verification model should be surfaced clearly so the team knows it is a policy change, not just a display issue. For collaborative handoff, the receiving team should get a concise summary for a normal completed run, but much more detail for partial runs, reruns, or mixed-source jobs, including what was processed, what was skipped, exact job state, boundaries of each processed segment, and warnings about data that may not compare cleanly across sources. At first-point triage, the process should capture the exact job parameters, source and target identifiers, tool version, relevant configuration in effect at the time, key logs, the error message or failure point, any local overrides or access context that may have changed behavior, and ideally a small reproducible sample or a pointer to the affected record set so another person can test it in a controlled setup. Each output package should keep a top-level trace link back to the original source repository, and individual records or files should carry their own trace references if the conversion splits or rearranges content in a way that would otherwise make provenance unclear. If the package is simple and one-to-one, the package-level link may be enough, but once things are aggregated or transformed, finer-grained traceability is needed. If the original source location is unavailable or has moved, the tool should preserve whatever stable identifier or archived reference was available at conversion time and mark the live location as unresolved rather than inventing a replacement.

slots.key: Result handling for borderline or invalid validation outcomes
slots.value: A batch is only successful when required conversion and verification steps are complete for everything in scope; small, understood exceptions may be explicitly accepted by the workflow, but not quietly ignored. slots.key: Source validation and triage before or during conversion
slots.value: Automatic fix-up should be limited to small, well-understood issues like minor formatting irregularities that don’t change the meaning of the record, or missing bits that can be safely normalized. Anything that suggests corruption, truncated content, broken headers, or ambiguous metadata should go to staff triage so a person decides rather than silently changing something important. Validation errors can be tolerated only if they are non-fatal and clearly documented, and only when the tool can preserve enough context for later review; if there is any risk the output would be misleading or not trustworthy, the process should stop or require explicit confirmation before continuing. The tool can often continue automatically when there are redirects, embedded resources, duplicate captures, or slightly unusual formatting, but truncated, corrupt, or contradictory records that affect trust should trigger human review. For reporting and verification, metadata should at minimum include the record identifier, capture date and time, source file or batch, record type, target URI or URL, and size or checksum information when available; conversion status, warnings, and the relationship between the source record and output record should also be shown for lineage tracing. Redirect location, duplicate match information, and incomplete-record flags become especially important in those cases, and if a record is incomplete or duplicated those details must be visible so users understand why the tool made its decision. Odd record layouts, embedded or nested content, and malformed ARC files that don't quite follow the expected structure should be planned for; some records may be passed through with warnings, while others may fail cleanly if integrity can't be preserved.
